"I'm timing contractions using BabyCenter's My Pregnancy & Baby Today app. Here's what's happening!"

"

Timing your contractions

A contraction is the tightening of the uterine muscles. Women experience contractions in all kinds of ways, ranging from cramping to tightening, burning, backache, and more.

When you’re in true labor, contractions get progressively longer, stronger, more painful, and closer together.

Our contraction timer will help you keep track of what you’re experiencing. When a contraction begins, press “Start contraction,” and when it ends, press “Stop contraction.” We’ll record the info for you and calculate the length of your contractions and the time between them – and the averages, too.

Typically, when you’re having your first baby, your doctor or midwife will want you to call once you’ve spent at least one hour having contractions that come five minutes apart and last one minute each. But your caregiver might have different instructions for you, so discuss the plan ahead of time.

Keep in mind that if your water breaks during the early part of labor, things may progress quickly from there. Notify your caregiver right away.

If this isn’t your first baby, you’ve experienced a fast labor before, or you’re already somewhat dilated and effaced, you may need to notify your caregiver as soon as you begin to have painful contractions."

Download the app: https://www.babycenter.com/my-pregnancy-today-app"

"Pick a time when your baby is active. Press Start timer, then the Kick! button every time you feel your baby kick, turn, or move. The tool tracks how long it takes to record 10 movements and saves each session so you can see how they compare.
Try to count kicks around the same time every day. If you notice a major change, call your health provider. If you don't reach 10 movements in two hours, try to perk up your baby by eating a snack, drinking something cold, or walking around. Wait an hour and count kicks again. If you still don't reach 10 in two hours, call your provider.
Why count kicks? Getting to know your baby's movement pattern can help you catch a problem early and may reduce the risk of stillbirth. Some practitioners advise starting daily kick counts at 28 weeks (or sooner if you have a high-risk pregnancy). There are lots of different methods for doing a kick count, so find out what your practitioner recommends."
